# Precise yes/no checklists and an AI grader: reliability, validity, and what a checklist cannot see

David S. Porcaro, Learning Design Alliance

Research and writing carried out with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic). See AI use.

# Abstract

Researchers at Google recently proposed replacing each criterion of a rating-scale (Likert) rubric with a list of precise yes/no questions, for evaluating AI answers to health questions. They reported that raters then agreed with each other more often, in about half the time. Educators who use AI models to grade student work could make the same change. This study asks three questions about it. Does a yes/no checklist make an AI grader's scores more consistent? Do the scores still match human graders' judgments? Does the checklist notice errors in a student's answer?

Two AI models (Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and GPT-5.4 mini) graded the same student work twice in each format. The rating-scale format used the original rubric. The checklist was written by a third AI model from the same rubric, and its score was the share of questions answered yes. The work came from two sources: 620 short answers from a university data-structures course, each scored by two human graders, and 272 first-year Java programming assignments (226 usable), each scored by three or four human graders. To test what each format notices, either a false sentence or a sentence that only lists the right technical terms was added to real answers, and the score was compared with adding a neutral sentence of the same length. The main analyses and their decision rules were fixed before any grading; one follow-up analysis was added after the main results were in.

There was no evidence that the checklist made scores more consistent. On the programming assignments the models tracked the human graders weakly or not at all on three of the four rubric dimensions, so the formats could not be compared there, and the comparison on the fourth was too uncertain to call. For the two models tested, a yes/no checklist did not make AI grading measurably more consistent, and a checklist built from a model answer mostly checked whether the expected ideas were present, not whether the answer was correct.

# 1. Introduction

Rubrics are how a grader's judgment is made explicit, and a rubric's format decides what that judgment can see. A Likert rubric asks for one rating per criterion on an ordered scale, often with a descriptor for each level. A checklist asks a series of yes/no questions and counts the answers. The choice between them is old in human assessment. It has become pressing again because large language models now grade student work at scale, and the format of the rubric is one of the few things an educator controls when a model does the grading.

The case for checklists is reliability. A yes/no question about one observable thing is easier to answer the same way twice than a rating on a five-point scale, and a grader whose scores do not repeat cannot be trusted with anything else. Mallinar et al. (2026) made this case for evaluating health language models. They decomposed each Likert criterion into many precise yes/no questions ("Precise Boolean rubrics"), and reported higher agreement between raters, including automated raters, in about half the rating time. A framework from a large research organization, with a clear mechanism and a reported gain, is the kind of evidence that changes practice. Educators building LLM grading for their own courses can reasonably read it as a recommendation.

Reliability is necessary for a score's validity but is not sufficient for it. A score can repeat perfectly and still measure the wrong thing. The question for an educator is therefore two-sided: whether the checklist makes the grader more consistent, and whether the consistent score is still a score of the student's understanding. The second half has particular force for checklists written from a reference answer, because such a checklist asks whether the expected ideas are present. An answer can contain every expected idea and also a false claim, or it can name every expected term without understanding any of them.

This paper adds a direct test of that trade for LLM graders of student work. It compares the two formats on identical inputs, with two models and repeated calls, against human raters, and with defects planted into real answers so that what each format can see is known by construction. The setting is deliberately the one educators face: short answers graded against a reference answer, and programs graded against a published rubric.

# 2. Background

# 2.1 Checklists and global ratings in human assessment

Medical education has compared checklists with global rating scales for more than thirty years, mostly in objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs), where an examiner watches a student perform a clinical task. A checklist lists specific actions, and the examiner marks each one as done or not done (for example, "asked about allergies"). A global rating scale instead asks the examiner for an overall judgment of the performance on one or a few ordered scales, such as overall competence rated from 1 to 5, usually with a short description of each level. The checklist corresponds to this study's yes/no checklist, and the global rating to its Likert format. Van der Vleuten, Norman and De Graaff (1991) argued that making a scoring instrument more objective, by splitting judgment into many observable items, does not by itself make scores more reliable. The companion paper (Norman, Van der Vleuten & De Graaff, 1991) took up the same question for validity.

The comparative studies that followed mostly agree. Cunnington, Neville and Norman (1996) found global ratings as reliable as checklists. Regehr, MacRae, Reznick and Szalay (1998) found global ratings more reliable across stations and better at separating levels of training. Hodges, Regehr, McNaughton, Tiberius and Hanson (1999) found that experienced clinicians scored lower than residents on checklists while scoring higher on global ratings. A systematic review of simulation-based assessment (Ilgen, Ma, Hatala & Cook, 2015) found similar inter-rater reliability for the two formats, higher inter-station reliability for global ratings, and a pooled correlation of 0.76 between them. A recent high-stakes OSCE (Ibrahim et al., 2026) found the two formats correlated at 0.924, yet the checklist failed no student at any station while the global rating found failures at four.

The opposing evidence comes from scoring rubrics in education. A holistic rubric gives the whole piece of work one overall score. An analytic rubric scores each criterion separately, each on its own scale, and then combines the scores. A topic-specific rubric is written for one task rather than for a type of task. In this study the Likert format is holistic for the short answers (one score per answer) and analytic for the programs (one score for each of four dimensions); the checklist splits each criterion further, into yes/no checks. Jonsson and Svingby (2007) reviewed rubric studies and found that analytic, topic-specific rubrics do raise the reliability of human scoring. Panadero and Jonsson (2020) reviewed 27 publications that criticize rubrics and grouped their criticisms into six themes. With a few exceptions, they found the evidence behind the criticisms neither direct nor strong: critics often relied on anecdote or personal experience, and often had a narrow idea of rubrics in mind, such as their use only in high-stakes summative testing. They called for the limitations of rubrics to be tested empirically. Their review weighs the evidence offered for the criticisms; it does not show that the criticisms are wrong. Barkaoui (2011) showed that the two kinds of reliability can part: in human essay raters, holistic scoring gave higher agreement between raters while analytic scoring gave higher self-consistency. Sadler (2009) gave the theoretical objection: a judgment of quality is not the sum of preset criteria, so a decomposition can miss properties of the whole. Humphry and Heldsinger (2014) showed that the structure of a rubric can itself threaten validity.

Two design traditions address what a checklist misses. Page and Bordage (1995) proposed scoring only the key features of a case, the critical decisions on which success turns. Homer, Fuller, Hallam and Pell (2020) showed that weighting checklist items changes the outcome for many borderline candidates. Both point to items that decide a score rather than count toward it.

# 2.2 Checklists and decomposed rubrics for LLM judges

Work on LLMs as evaluators of generated text has moved in the same direction as Mallinar et al. (2026). CheckEval (Lee et al., 2025) scores text with checklists of yes/no questions and reports higher agreement across models. TICK (Cook et al., 2024) has a model generate an instruction-specific checklist and reports higher agreement with humans. InFoBench (Qin et al., 2024) decomposes instructions into requirements, and FLASK (Ye et al., 2024) decomposes evaluation into skills. Both report more reliable evaluation. HealthBench (Arora et al., 2025) grades model responses against physician-written rubric criteria with positive and negative weights. Likert-style scoring with an LLM has its own baseline in G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023), and LLM-Rubric (Hashemi et al., 2024) calibrates rubric answers to human judgments.

Most of these gains were measured where agreement started low. The evidence that decomposition can weaken validity is thinner and recent. Furuhashi, Nakayama, Kodama and Sugawara (2025) gave LLM judges generated checklists in two settings: pairwise comparison, where the judge picks the better of two responses, and direct scoring, where it gives one response a score on a scale, as a grader does. The checklists helped pairwise comparison, but their benefit was less consistent for direct scoring. Zhang (2026) compared atomic and holistic LLM judges under matched prompts. Decomposing the candidate answer did worse than a holistic judge where the label depends on completeness, while decomposing the reference, checking whether each reference claim is covered, did better; what a judge decomposes should follow what the label measures. Kucia, Chakraborty and Wróblewska (2026) found that longer rubric-style prompts scored essays worse than short keyword prompts. Deng, Farber, Lee and Tang (2025) varied a different property, the number of grade categories rather than any decomposition of a criterion. On a short-answer benchmark, an LLM grader agreed well with experts when it chose between two labels (correct or incorrect) and less well as the label set grew to three and five categories.

The nearest comparisons against an independent human reference were made on other material. DeLucia et al. (2026) compared a general Likert judge, an analytic rubric and a dynamic checklist against clinicians' completeness labels on health-chatbot responses, including HealthBench, and found all of them near chance. On student programs, Pathak et al. (2025) found that grading one rubric point per call agreed less with teaching assistants than grading against the whole rubric, and was harsher. Sonkar et al. (2024) scored long chemistry answers as yes/no entailment of each rubric item and reported it better than predicting a score. No study found here compares a yes/no checklist with a Likert rubric on student short answers against independent human raters, or compares formats at matched reliability.

# 2.3 Presence-based scoring and its vulnerabilities

A checklist written from a reference answer is a form of presence-based scoring: it asks whether expected content appears. Automated short-answer scoring has used this design for two decades. c-rater (Leacock & Chodorow, 2003) scored answers by the concepts they contain, and similarity-based graders, including the one built on the Mohler corpus used here (Mohler, Bunescu & Mihalcea, 2011), score by overlap with a reference.

Presence-based scorers are known to be gameable. Powers et al. (2002) found that experts could raise e-rater's scores more easily than lower them. Ding et al. (2020) found that content-scoring systems accepted many answers made of shuffled words. Filighera, Steuer and Rensing (2020) and Filighera, Ochs, Steuer and Tregel (2024) found short-answer graders fooled by inserted words. Kabra et al. (2020) found essay scorers overstable to added content. Yarmohammadtoosky et al. (2025) reported defenses for short-answer graders. For LLM scorers, Walsh and Ivan (2026) tested robustness to construct-irrelevant factors, and Doddapaneni et al. (2024) planted errors in text to find what LLM evaluators miss, a behavioral-testing approach from Ribeiro et al. (2020).

In Messick's (1994, 1995) terms, a score that misses a false claim underrepresents the construct, and a score raised by terms used without understanding carries construct-irrelevant variance. Kane's (2013) validity argument frames both as failures of the scoring inference, the first step from a performance to a score. Cook, Brydges, Ginsburg and Hatala (2015) give a practical guide to that argument for assessment.

# 3. Research questions

  • RQ1. When an LLM grader scores student work with a checklist of precise yes/no checks instead of a Likert rubric written from the same criterion, are its scores more reliable, across repeated calls and across two models?
  • RQ2. Do the checklist scores track human raters as well as the Likert scores do, and if not, where on the human scale do the two formats part?
  • RQ3. When a false sentence, or a sentence of key terms without understanding, is added to a real answer, does the checklist score change as the Likert score does, and which checks carry the change?

# 4. Method

# 4.1 Design

Every sampled item was graded in two formats, by two models, twice each, on identical inputs. The grader in each format is the prompt plus the model, and the two formats differ only in what the model is asked to return. The Likert grader returns one score per criterion on the corpus's own scale. The checklist grader returns YES or NO to each check, and its score for a criterion is the share of YES, unweighted, as in Mallinar et al. (2026). Each item is its own control.

The design, the thresholds, the predictions and the verdict strings were registered in the analysis script before any model call. The instruments, the checklists and the planted sentences, were written, hashed and frozen before any grading call. A detection floor was run first on synthetic graders shaped like the data (§4.6, Appendix A.2). A second analysis (RQ2's comparison by band of human score and RQ3's per-check attribution) was chosen after the primary results had been read, from the literature review, and registered before any of its own estimates were computed. It is a follow-up, not part of the original registration, and it makes no model call.

# 4.2 Data

Short answers. The Mohler corpus (Mohler, Bunescu & Mihalcea, 2011; released under CC BY 4.0) holds answers by undergraduates to questions from a data-structures course. Each question has an instructor's reference answer, and each answer was scored 0–5 by two raters independently. Exercises 11 and 12 were dropped because their per-rater scores are on another scale, which leaves 1,721 answers to 62 questions. The main draw takes up to 10 answers per question in a fixed hashed order: 620 answers over 62 questions. The two raters' scores correlate at 0.621 on this draw (95% interval 0.546 to 0.689, resampling questions).

Programs. The Menagerie corpus (Messer, Brown, Kolling & Shi, 2024; CC BY 4.0) holds first-year Java coursework submissions re-graded by recruited raters on four dimensions (Correctness, Code Elegance, Readability, Documentation). Each dimension uses a 14-level letter scale and the six-band rubric the raters were given. Every submission with source code and at least three grades on every dimension was used: 272 submissions. Their source files were concatenated and cut at 90,000 characters, which shortened 73 of them, identically for both formats. Neither format sees the coursework specification, so Correctness cannot be judged against the assignment's requirements.

# 4.3 The two formats

Likert. For a short answer, the grader saw the question, the reference answer and the student's answer, and returned a score from 0 to 5 in steps of 0.5. For a program, it saw each dimension's definition and its six rubric bands, and returned one letter grade per dimension.

Checklist. A third model, GPT-5.5, wrote the checklists before any grading. For each Mohler question it wrote three to eight checks from the question and the reference answer. For each Menagerie dimension it wrote five to twelve checks from the dimension's definition and bands. The prompt asked for checks about one thing each, answerable from the student's work, all YES for a fully correct answer, and phrased so that YES is desirable. It neither asked for nor forbade checks that look for errors. The result was 284 checks over 62 questions (three to seven each) and 10 to 12 checks per programming dimension. The checklist grader saw everything the Likert grader saw except the scale and the band descriptors, which the checks replaced.

Most checks ask whether something the reference answer expects is present, for example whether the answer says that a stack removes the most recently added item first. These are presence checks. The checklist author also wrote, unprompted, checks that ask whether the answer avoids a particular mistake, for example whether it avoids describing a stack's removal order as first-in-first-out. These are error checks. A word rule marks them: a check is an error check when its wording contains "avoid", which is how the registration names them (its verdicts read AVOID-CHECKS-…). The rule was fixed after the checklists were read and before any grading call. A second rule, registered before the checklists were written, marks a no-error check: a check whose wording says the answer avoids, or contains no, incorrect claim, error, mistake or misconception. The registration predicted that such checks would catch a false sentence added to an answer (§4.5), and so narrow the gap between how much the checklist and the Likert format penalized it. Eight of the 284 checks match it, and all eight are also error checks, each naming a mistake specific to its question, so the no-error checks are a subset of the error checks.

# 4.4 Models and calls

The two models were Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite, called directly through Google's API with its default sampling, and GPT-5.4 mini, called directly through OpenAI's API with low reasoning effort. Each item was graded twice per format per model, as independent calls. The model that served each call was recorded, and every call was served by the model requested. In all, 10,976 gradings were made, and none failed.

GPT-5.4 mini returned a wrong number of answers in 46 of its 544 checklist calls on programs (8.5%), on 45 submissions, for example 12 answers to Readability's 10 checks. One Gemini Likert call on a program also did not parse. By the rule registered in advance, a submission with any unparseable call leaves every programming table, which keeps 226 of 272 submissions. No short-answer call failed to parse.

# 4.5 Planted defects

For RQ3, 120 short answers the raters scored highly (mean at least 4.5) and 120 they scored low (mean at most 2.5) were drawn, at most three per question. For each answer GPT-5.5 wrote two sentences to append, in the student's voice:

  • High answers. A false sentence making a specific claim that contradicts the reference answer's key point.
  • Low answers. A key-terms sentence naming the reference answer's technical terms without stating the correct relationship between them.
  • Both. A neutral sentence that is true and adds no claim about the question's key ideas.

Each answer was graded twice in each format with the treatment appended and twice with the neutral sentence appended, never in its original form. The contrast is therefore matched in position and, closely, in length. Neutral sentences averaged 0.963 (false-sentence pairs) and 0.968 (key-terms pairs) of the treatment's length, and every neutral sentence was within 0.75 to 1.33 times its own treatment's length.

Gemini 3.1 Pro, as a manipulation checker, checked each pair. A model check is not a human one, and it is reported as such. All 120 false-sentence pairs passed; 112 of 120 key-terms pairs passed. The analysis uses the passing pairs.

# 4.6 Measures and analysis

Every score is put on a 0–1 scale: the Likert score over the scale maximum, and the checklist share of YES. Each item's score is the mean of its two calls, except in test–retest reliability. Each measure is described here in words; Appendix A gives its formula.

Reliability and validity. Reliability is a measure agreeing with itself. Test–retest reliability is Pearson's correlation (r) between a model's two gradings of the same items, and cross-model reliability is r between the two models' scores. Validity is not a single number here. It is the case that a score means what it is taken to mean, and the study gathers three kinds of evidence for it (Messick, 1995): whether the scores agree with the human raters, where in the range of answers they part from them, and whether the scores respond to what the task is about and not to what it is not (the planted defects). Agreement with the human raters, or human agreement, is r between a format's scores and the mean human score, read beside the raters' agreement with each other, because the human score is itself an unreliable reference.

Differences between formats. Each comparison is a difference between the formats, taken as checklist minus Likert, so a positive difference favors the checklist. dR and dX are the differences in test–retest and cross-model reliability and answer RQ1 (Table 1). dH is the difference in human agreement and answers RQ2 (Table 2). The registration called this measure validity, so its verdicts read LIKERT-MORE-VALID and BOOLEAN-MORE-VALID. dH and dR are averaged over the two models and also reported for each model; dX compares the two models' scores directly.

Planted defects. D is how much a format's score changed when a planted sentence was added to an answer, against the same answer with a neutral sentence of matched length. A negative D means the score fell. C is the checklist's D minus the Likert D. For a false sentence, a positive C means the checklist registered less of the error; for key terms without understanding, it means the checklist gave the terms more credit. C answers RQ3 (Table 4). Because the checklist score is a share of YES answers, its D splits exactly into the part that came from its error checks (E) and the part from its presence checks (P). S is the error checks' share of the checklist's loss, and K is how much less the same answers would have lost if they had been scored on their presence checks alone (Table 5).

By band of human score. In the short-answer assessments, a format's signed error on an answer is its score minus the human mean on the same scale, so a positive error credits the answer more than the raters did. G is the checklist's error minus the Likert format's within each band of human score. It shows where in the range of answers the formats part, which a correlation cannot (RQ2, Table 3).

Intervals and verdicts. Intervals are 95% intervals from a bootstrap that resamples whole questions for short answers, because answers to one question share a reference and a checklist, and whole submissions for programs. The verdicts were registered with their margins. A difference is clear when its 95% interval excludes zero: the data then show which format did better, and the verdict names it. Otherwise it is EQUIVALENT if its 90% interval lies inside the margin (±0.05 for human agreement, ±0.03 for reliability), meaning any difference is too small to matter, and UNRESOLVED if not, meaning the data are too uncertain to call either way.

The detection floor. Before any model call, the analysis was run on simulated graders built on the real answers and human scores, with effects of known size planted in them, to check that it finds those effects and does not invent others (Appendix A). It passed after one revision, and showed two limits that bear on the results. First, a format with fewer possible scores looks less reliable even when its judgments are equally consistent: two gradings near a boundary between scores round to different values, and wider steps make each such jump larger. The checklist has fewer possible scores than the Likert format, and in a simulation that gave the checklist seven possible scores (six checks) this alone produced a spurious "Likert more reliable" verdict in 22.5% (short-answer assessments) and 23.5% (assessments of software programs) of runs. The short-answer checklists actually used had four to eight possible scores, close to the simulation. The program checklists had 11 to 13 against the Likert format's 14, so on programs the grid can explain much less of the difference than 23.5% suggests. Second, with this many programs a difference in human agreement of 0.10 is found only 56–58% of the time, so an UNRESOLVED verdict on programs does not rule out differences up to about 0.15. In the short-answer assessments a difference of 0.08 is found 95–97% of the time.

Ethics and data. Both corpora are public and released under CC BY 4.0. They were used under the organization's protocol for open graded corpora. No student was contacted, and no human grade was sent to a model. Student answers and programs were sent to the two models that graded them, and short answers to the checklist author and the manipulation checker.

Table 1. Reliability at the response level. Test–retest is r between a model's two calls; cross-model is r between the two models' mean scores. dR is the checklist-minus-Likert difference in test–retest, averaged over the two models; dX is the difference in cross-model r. Intervals resample questions (Mohler, n = 620) or submissions (Menagerie, n = 226).

Figure 1. Reliability from Table 1 as slope charts. In each panel a line runs from a model's r under the Likert format (left) to its r under the checklist (right), so a falling line means the checklist was less reliable. Top row: test–retest r for each model (solid Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite, dashed GPT-5.4 mini). Bottom row: cross-model r, one line. Under each panel are the pooled difference and its verdict, in bold where the data clearly show a difference. Source: code/studies/measurement/grader-boolean-rubrics/out/results.json.

Re-run this finding Recompute Table 1's reliability estimates and the per-tuple ICC from the published per-case file (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook and download the data file (per-case-model-outputs.jsonl.gz) into the same folder, then run all cells. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: reliability of the two formats (RQ1)

This notebook recomputes the point estimates of Table 1 and the per-tuple ICC from the per-case file published with release checklist-grading-2026, and nothing else: no model call, no corpus. It needs Python 3.9+ with numpy, and per-case-model-outputs.jsonl beside this notebook (or in RELEASE_DIR). The 95% intervals come from a 4,000-replicate cluster bootstrap in the release's code package; this notebook checks the point estimates.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "checklist-grading-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


print("Data:", shown(find_release_file()))
Data: per-case-model-outputs.jsonl

import json
import numpy as np

recs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(find_release_file(), encoding="utf-8")]
G = {(r["corpus"], r["id"], r["form"], r["model"], r["arm"], r["rep"]): r for r in recs if r["record"] == "grade"}
items = {(r["corpus"], r["id"]): r for r in recs if r["record"] == "item"}
MODELS, ARMS, REPS = ("gemini", "gpt"), ("likert", "boolean"), (0, 1)
DIMS = ["Correctness", "Code Elegance", "Readability", "Documentation"]

def val(corpus, i, m, a, k, dim=None):
    g = G.get((corpus, i, "orig", m, a, k))
    if g is None:
        return None
    return g["score"] if dim is None else (g["scores"] or {}).get(dim)

def complete(corpus, ids, dim=None):
    return [i for i in ids if all(val(corpus, i, m, a, k, dim) is not None for m in MODELS for a in ARMS for k in REPS)]

r = lambda x, y: float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])
mohler = sorted(i for (c, i), it in items.items() if c == "mohler" and "main" in it["draws"])
men = sorted((i for (c, i) in items if c == "menagerie"), key=int)
print(len(mohler), "short answers;", len(men), "programs")
620 short answers; 272 programs

def table(corpus, ids, dim=None):
    ids = complete(corpus, ids, DIMS[0] if dim else None)
    x = {(m, a, k): np.array([val(corpus, i, m, a, k, dim) for i in ids]) for m in MODELS for a in ARMS for k in REPS}
    R = {(m, a): r(x[m, a, 0], x[m, a, 1]) for m in MODELS for a in ARMS}
    X = {a: r((x["gemini", a, 0] + x["gemini", a, 1]) / 2, (x["gpt", a, 0] + x["gpt", a, 1]) / 2) for a in ARMS}
    dR = np.mean([R[m, "boolean"] - R[m, "likert"] for m in MODELS])
    return len(ids), R, X, dR, X["boolean"] - X["likert"]

rows = {"Mohler short answers": table("mohler", mohler)}
for d in DIMS:
    rows[f"Menagerie {d}"] = table("menagerie", men, d)
for name, (n, R, X, dR, dX) in rows.items():
    print(f"{name:24s} n={n}  retest L/B gemini {R['gemini','likert']:.3f}/{R['gemini','boolean']:.3f}  "
          f"gpt {R['gpt','likert']:.3f}/{R['gpt','boolean']:.3f}  dR {dR:+.3f}  cross L/B {X['likert']:.3f}/{X['boolean']:.3f}  dX {dX:+.3f}")

Table 1's point estimates reproduce.

# Per-tuple ICC(3,1) between the two models (the health framework's unit) against response-level.
def icc31(Y):
    n, k = Y.shape
    gm = Y.mean()
    ssr = k * ((Y.mean(1) - gm) ** 2).sum()
    ssc = n * ((Y.mean(0) - gm) ** 2).sum()
    sse = ((Y - gm) ** 2).sum() - ssr - ssc
    msr, mse = ssr / (n - 1), sse / ((n - 1) * (k - 1))
    return (msr - mse) / (msr + (k - 1) * mse)

ids = complete("mohler", mohler)
tuples = []
for i in ids:
    for k in REPS:
        tuples += list(zip(G[("mohler", i, "orig", "gemini", "boolean", k)]["checks"],
                           G[("mohler", i, "orig", "gpt", "boolean", k)]["checks"]))
tup = icc31(np.array(tuples, float))
resp = {a: icc31(np.array([[val("mohler", i, "gemini", a, k), val("mohler", i, "gpt", a, k)] for k in REPS for i in ids]))
        for a in ARMS}
print(f"per (answer, check) tuple {tup:.3f}; per answer: checklist {resp['boolean']:.3f}, Likert {resp['likert']:.3f}")
assert (f"{tup:.3f}", f"{resp['boolean']:.3f}", f"{resp['likert']:.3f}") == ("0.803", "0.889", "0.865")
print("The per-tuple ICC reproduces.")

Re-run: agreement with the human raters (RQ2)

This notebook recomputes the point estimates of Table 2 (each format's correlation with the human mean, the human ceiling, and the difference dH) and of Table 3 (signed error by band of human score) from the per-case file published with release checklist-grading-2026. It needs Python 3.9+ with numpy and per-case-model-outputs.jsonl beside this notebook (or in RELEASE_DIR). The 95% intervals come from the release code package's 4,000-replicate cluster bootstrap; this notebook checks the point estimates.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "checklist-grading-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


print("Data:", shown(find_release_file()))
Data: per-case-model-outputs.jsonl

import json
import numpy as np

recs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(find_release_file(), encoding="utf-8")]
G = {(r["corpus"], r["id"], r["form"], r["model"], r["arm"], r["rep"]): r for r in recs if r["record"] == "grade"}
items = {(r["corpus"], r["id"]): r for r in recs if r["record"] == "item"}
MODELS, ARMS, REPS = ("gemini", "gpt"), ("likert", "boolean"), (0, 1)
DIMS = ["Correctness", "Code Elegance", "Readability", "Documentation"]
r = lambda x, y: float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])

def val(corpus, i, m, a, k, dim=None):
    g = G.get((corpus, i, "orig", m, a, k))
    return None if g is None else (g["score"] if dim is None else (g["scores"] or {}).get(dim))

def complete(corpus, ids, dim=None):
    return [i for i in ids if all(val(corpus, i, m, a, k, dim) is not None for m in MODELS for a in ARMS for k in REPS)]

def mean_score(corpus, i, m, a, dim=None):
    return (val(corpus, i, m, a, 0, dim) + val(corpus, i, m, a, 1, dim)) / 2
mohler = complete("mohler", sorted(i for (c, i), it in items.items() if c == "mohler" and "main" in it["draws"]))
h = np.array([items["mohler", i]["h"] for i in mohler])
V = {(m, a): r(np.array([mean_score("mohler", i, m, a) for i in mohler]), h) for m in MODELS for a in ARMS}
dV = np.mean([V[m, "boolean"] - V[m, "likert"] for m in MODELS])
ceiling = r([items["mohler", i]["g1"] for i in mohler], [items["mohler", i]["g2"] for i in mohler])
print(f"Mohler n={len(mohler)}: gemini {V['gemini','likert']:.3f}/{V['gemini','boolean']:.3f}, "
      f"gpt {V['gpt','likert']:.3f}/{V['gpt','boolean']:.3f}, dH {dV:+.3f}, raters {ceiling:.3f}")
assert (f"{V['gemini','likert']:.3f}", f"{V['gemini','boolean']:.3f}", f"{V['gpt','likert']:.3f}",
        f"{V['gpt','boolean']:.3f}", f"{dV:+.3f}", f"{ceiling:.3f}") == ("0.764", "0.688", "0.819", "0.682", "-0.106", "0.621")
Mohler n=620: gemini 0.764/0.688, gpt 0.819/0.682, dH -0.106, raters 0.621

men = complete("menagerie", sorted((i for (c, i) in items if c == "menagerie"), key=int), DIMS[0])
PRINTED = {"Correctness": ("0.405", "0.433", "-0.173", "-0.054", "+0.073", "0.622"),
           "Code Elegance": ("0.035", "0.017", "-0.182", "-0.137", "+0.013", "0.539"),
           "Readability": ("0.039", "-0.007", "-0.235", "-0.011", "+0.089", "0.571"),
           "Documentation": ("0.286", "0.079", "-0.284", "-0.125", "-0.024", "0.525")}
for d in DIMS:
    hm = np.array([items["menagerie", i]["h"][d] for i in men])
    Vd = {(m, a): r(np.array([mean_score("menagerie", i, m, a, d) for i in men]), hm) for m in MODELS for a in ARMS}
    dVd = np.mean([Vd[m, "boolean"] - Vd[m, "likert"] for m in MODELS])
    one, rest = [], []                      # one rater against the mean of the others, pooled over ratings
    for i in men:
        g = items["menagerie", i]["raters"][d]
        for j in range(len(g)):
            one.append(g[j]); rest.append(np.mean(g[:j] + g[j + 1:]))
    got = (f"{Vd['gemini','likert']:.3f}", f"{Vd['gemini','boolean']:.3f}", f"{Vd['gpt','likert']:.3f}",
           f"{Vd['gpt','boolean']:.3f}", f"{dVd:+.3f}", f"{r(one, rest):.3f}")
    print(f"Menagerie {d:14s} n={len(men)}: {got}")
    assert got == PRINTED[d], (d, got)
print("Table 2's point estimates reproduce.")

# Table 3: signed error (score minus human mean / 5), pooled over models and calls, by band of human score.
eL = np.array([np.mean([val("mohler", i, m, "likert", k) for m in MODELS for k in REPS]) for i in mohler]) - h / 5
eB = np.array([np.mean([val("mohler", i, m, "boolean", k) for m in MODELS for k in REPS]) for i in mohler]) - h / 5
BANDS = {"LOW": h <= 2.5, "MID": (h > 2.5) & (h < 4.5), "HIGH": h >= 4.5}
PRINTED3 = {"LOW": (65, "-0.144", "-0.123", "+0.022"), "MID": (145, "-0.149", "-0.327", "-0.178"),
            "HIGH": (410, "-0.049", "-0.160", "-0.111")}
for b, mask in BANDS.items():
    got = (int(mask.sum()), f"{eL[mask].mean():+.3f}", f"{eB[mask].mean():+.3f}", f"{eB[mask].mean() - eL[mask].mean():+.3f}")
    print(b, got)
    assert got == PRINTED3[b], (b, got)
print("Table 3's point estimates reproduce.")

Because the shortfall is largest in the middle band, it narrows the distance between partly correct and wrong answers, which is consistent with the lower correlation. Band means do not decompose a correlation, and disagreement within bands was not measured.

Answer to RQ2. No. In the short-answer assessments the checklist agreed less with the human raters than the Likert format, for both models. It under-credited partly and fully correct answers, which is consistent with that loss, and it was not shown to over-credit wrong ones. In the assessments of software programs the question could not be answered, because the models tracked the raters weakly or not at all on most dimensions.

Re-run: planted defects and which checks carry them (RQ3)

This notebook recomputes the point estimates of Table 4 (each format's change when a false or key-terms sentence replaces a length-matched neutral sentence on the same answer) and Table 5 (the checklist's change split into its error checks and its presence checks) from the per-case file published with release checklist-grading-2026. It needs Python 3.9+ with numpy and per-case-model-outputs.jsonl beside this notebook (or in RELEASE_DIR).

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "checklist-grading-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


print("Data:", shown(find_release_file()))
Data: per-case-model-outputs.jsonl

import json
import numpy as np

recs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(find_release_file(), encoding="utf-8")]
G = {(r["id"], r["form"], r["model"], r["arm"], r["rep"]): r for r in recs if r["record"] == "grade" and r["corpus"] == "mohler"}
items = {r["id"]: r for r in recs if r["record"] == "item" and r["corpus"] == "mohler"}
Q = {r["q"]: r for r in recs if r["record"] == "question" and r["corpus"] == "mohler"}
MODELS, ARMS, REPS = ("gemini", "gpt"), ("likert", "boolean"), (0, 1)

def answers(kind):
    return [i for i, it in sorted(items.items()) if kind in it and it[kind]["ok"] and it[kind]["manip_pass"]]

def score(i, form, m, a):
    return np.mean([G[i, form, m, a, k]["score"] for k in REPS])
PRINTED4 = {"contra": (120, "-0.473", "-0.172", "+0.302"), "stuff": (112, "+0.273", "+0.348", "+0.075")}
for kind, want in PRINTED4.items():
    ids = answers(kind)
    D = {a: np.mean([np.mean([score(i, f"{kind}-treat", m, a) - score(i, f"{kind}-neutral", m, a) for i in ids])
                     for m in MODELS]) for a in ARMS}
    got = (len(ids), f"{D['likert']:+.3f}", f"{D['boolean']:+.3f}", f"{D['boolean'] - D['likert']:+.3f}")
    print(kind, got)
    assert got == want, (kind, got)
print("Table 4's point estimates reproduce.")
contra (120, '-0.473', '-0.172', '+0.302')
stuff (112, '+0.273', '+0.348', '+0.075')
Table 4's point estimates reproduce.

def split(kind, subset=None):
    rows = []
    for i in answers(kind):
        avoid = np.array(Q[items[i]["q"]]["avoid_by_check"], bool)
        if subset is not None and avoid.any() != subset:
            continue
        per_m = []
        for m in MODELS:
            y = {f: np.mean([G[i, f"{kind}-{f}", m, "boolean", k]["checks"] for k in REPS], axis=0) for f in ("treat", "neutral")}
            d = y["treat"] - y["neutral"]
            per_m.append((d.sum() / len(d), d[avoid].sum() / len(d), d[~avoid].sum() / len(d)))
        rows.append(np.mean(per_m, axis=0))
    rows = np.array(rows)
    return len(rows), rows.mean(0)

n, (D, A, P) = split("contra")
print(f"false sentence, all: n={n} D {D:+.3f} A {A:+.3f} P {P:+.3f}")
assert (n, f"{D:+.3f}", f"{A:+.3f}", f"{P:+.3f}") == (120, "-0.172", "-0.109", "-0.063")
n, (D, A, P) = split("contra", True)
print(f"false sentence, with error checks: n={n} D {D:+.3f} E {A:+.3f} share {A / D:.3f}")
assert (n, f"{D:+.3f}", f"{A:+.3f}", f"{A / D:.3f}") == (77, "-0.224", "-0.170", "0.760")
n, (D, A, P) = split("contra", False)
print(f"false sentence, no error check: n={n} D {D:+.3f}")
assert (n, f"{D:+.3f}") == (43, "-0.079")
n, (D, A, P) = split("stuff")
print(f"key terms, all: n={n} D {D:+.3f} A {A:+.3f} P {P:+.3f}")
assert (n, f"{D:+.3f}", f"{A:+.3f}", f"{P:+.3f}") == (112, "+0.348", "+0.003", "+0.346")
print("Table 5's point estimates reproduce.")

Table 5. Which checks moved the checklist's score when a sentence was planted. Each row is a set of answers that received the planted sentence (§4.5): the 120 good answers given a false sentence, split in the middle two rows by whether the question's checklist had any error check, and the 112 weak answers given a sentence of key terms. D is the change in the checklist score against the same answer with a neutral sentence; E is the part of that change that came from the error checks (checks asking whether the answer avoids a particular mistake, §4.3) and P the part from the presence checks, so D = E + P. S is E divided by D. A blank cell is a value not reported for that row; the 43 answers have no error checks, so all of their change is P. In plain words, the verdicts say that presence checks registered the false sentence a little, that error checks carried most of the loss where they existed, and that the key-terms gain came from presence checks. Pooled over the two models; intervals resample questions. The two analyses draw separate bootstrap resamples, so an interval here can differ from Table 4's in the third decimal for the same point estimate.

# 6. Discussion

# 6.1 Interpretation

The results fit the human literature more closely than the recent LLM-judge literature. Checklists were not more reliable than global ratings for human examiners (Van der Vleuten et al., 1991; Regehr et al., 1998; Ilgen et al., 2015), and they were not shown to be for these two models either. The reliability gains reported for LLM checklists (Lee et al., 2025; Cook et al., 2024; Mallinar et al., 2026) were measured where agreement started low. Here, in the short-answer assessments, both models already gave nearly the same scores on a second grading with a Likert prompt, which left a checklist almost no room to improve consistency. In the assessments of software programs, where the models were not consistent, the checklist did not help either. This does not contradict Jonsson and Svingby's (2007) finding for human raters, but it gives no support to the idea that decomposition helps an inconsistent model grader.

The three kinds of validity evidence point the same way. The checklist agreed less with the human raters, and not because its scores varied more from call to call. The band analysis shows where it departed instead: it under-credited partial and complete answers, which parallels Hodges et al.'s (1999) finding for checklists scoring experts, and Sadler's (2009) argument that quality is not the sum of preset criteria. An LLM grader of student programs that checked one rubric point per call was likewise harsher than teaching assistants, because it withheld partial credit (Pathak et al., 2025).

The planted defects show the other half. A checklist written from a reference answer decomposes the reference, which suits a label about coverage (Zhang, 2026) but not one that also penalizes errors, as the Mohler raters' scores do. Most of its checks ask whether expected content is present, so content that is added, whether false or irrelevant, is outside what they ask about. In Messick's (1994) terms, the missed false claim is construct underrepresentation and the key-term gain is construct-irrelevant variance. The planted defects are the kind of empirical test of a rubric's limits that Panadero and Jonsson (2020) asked for, here for a model-written checklist read by an AI grader. The same pattern has been seen when rubric-based LLM judges are used as rewards: gains concentrated on presence-based criteria while factual correctness fell (Mahmoud et al., 2026).

The design implication is the one Page and Bordage (1995) drew for clinical cases, and LLM rubrics already provide for it: HealthBench weights some criteria negatively (Arora et al., 2025), and Rubrics as Rewards writes "pitfall" criteria for common errors, phrased so that meeting them is good, and marks some criteria as invalidating a response if missed (Gunjal et al., 2025). Here the error checks carried most of the loss, but as counted items, one vote among several, and they did not bring the checklist to the Likert format's sensitivity.

The checklist format also brought failures of its own that a Likert prompt does not have. Gemini's checklist answered YES to nearly every check on Code Elegance and Readability. That is not a general tendency to say yes: LLMs answering yes/no questions lean toward no (Braun, 2025). Those checks did not discriminate between submissions. GPT-5.4 mini returned the wrong number of answers in 8.5% of its checklist calls on programs, where each call carried 44 checks across four dimensions. That fits the finding that models lose track of instructions as their number grows (Jaroslawicz, Whiting, Shah & Maamari, 2025). A longer checklist is a longer list of instructions to follow in one reply.

The comparison with Mallinar et al. (2026) has a limit that should be stated plainly. That study measured agreement between raters, including human raters, on health-advice responses, and its abstract makes no claim about agreement with an independent reference. This study measured LLM graders on student work against human raters. The two results are not in conflict on reliability among human raters, which this study did not test. They differ on what a checklist is evidence for. A gain in agreement between raters is not a gain in validity, and the two should not be reported as one.

# 6.2 Implications for practice

A precise yes/no checklist should not be adopted for LLM grading on the expectation that it will make scores more consistent. Both models tested were already consistent with a Likert prompt when grading against a reference answer, and the checklist was not shown to improve on it (RQ1). In the assessments of software programs it was less consistent wherever the data clearly showed a difference.

A checklist written from a reference answer mostly measures whether the expected content is present, not whether the answer is right (RQ3). It can pass an answer that contains the right ideas and a false claim, and it can credit an answer that names the right terms without understanding them. An educator who uses one should write checks that look for the specific errors and misconceptions that matter, because most of what a checklist registered of a mistake came through such checks (RQ3). They may work better as items that decide or cap a score than as one vote among many, which remains to be tested.

A checklist score should not be read on the same scale as a holistic grade. It runs low for answers that are partly or fully correct (RQ2), so a pass mark set for one format will not transfer to the other.

Results reported for one population of raters, or for one kind of content, should not be carried to another without a check. A framework validated on health-advice responses and human raters does not by that fact apply to LLM graders of student work. The checks that matter are agreement with independent human graders and a planted error the grader must catch.

# 6.3 Implications for research

Reliability and validity should be reported separately for any change of rubric format. Where a format's reliability is compared, the unit (per response or per check) and the facet (repeated calls, different models, different human raters) should be named. A coarser output scale loses repeatability on its own (Bollen & Barb, 1981), and the detection floor showed that this is large enough to produce a spurious verdict here, so formats with different scales need that control.

Planted defects are an established test of evaluators (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Doddapaneni et al., 2024). With a size-matched neutral sentence on the same answer as the control, they are a cheap and direct test of what a scoring rubric can see, and they need no new human grading. They should accompany any proposal for a new rubric format.

Several questions are open. One is whether decisive error checks, items that cap or veto a score, close the gap that counted error checks only narrowed; rubric-based rewards mark such criteria but still aggregate them as weighted items (Gunjal et al., 2025). Another is whether learned weights over the checks recover the human agreement the unweighted share loses. These can be tested on the per-check answers this release publishes. Others need new data: whether the results hold for human raters using LLM-written checklists, and for stronger models on judgment-laden work such as the software programs here. Neither model graded the software programs well, so that question remains open.

# 7. Threats to validity

# 7.1 Construct validity

The checklists were written by one model, from one prompt, with no human review. A teacher writing checks by hand, or a different prompt, might produce checklists with more error checks or better coverage. The result is a result about model-written checklists of this kind, which is how such checklists are likely to be produced at scale, and not about analytic rubrics in general (Panadero & Jonsson, 2020).

The distinction between error checks and presence checks rests on a word rule over the checklist text. The rule was fixed before any grading call, and the attribution in Table 5 follows exactly from it. Checks that look for mistakes without the word "avoid" would be counted as presence checks, which would make the presence checks look more sensitive to errors than they are.

The planted sentences were written by one model and checked by another. A model check is not a person reading each pair. The false sentences are clear contradictions of the key point. Subtler errors, such as a wrong detail inside a mostly correct sentence, may be registered less often by both formats.

The human reference is itself unreliable. In the short-answer assessments the two raters agree at 0.621, and in the assessments of software programs the raters at 0.525 to 0.622. Agreement with the raters in Table 2 is attenuated by that unreliability for both formats alike. Attenuation scales both correlations by the same factor, so it can shrink the difference between the formats but not reverse its sign.

# 7.2 Internal validity

The two formats saw identical inputs except the scale and band descriptors, which the checks replaced. A Likert prompt carrying the bands' language and a checklist carrying the checks' language differ in more than format. That is inherent in the comparison, and it is the comparison an educator would make.

The 46 programs dropped for unparseable calls (45 of them for miscounted checklist answers) were not dropped at random. Every Menagerie estimate is on the remaining 226, and the format comparison there is uninformative for other reasons (§5.2).

# 7.3 External validity

Two small, inexpensive models were tested. Larger models might follow long checklists better and might grade the software programs. The short answers come from one course in one subject, with short reference answers; longer or more open questions may favor or disfavor checklists differently. No human rater used either format, so nothing here says how checklists affect human graders, the population Mallinar et al. (2026) studied.

# 7.4 Statistical conclusion validity

The intervals resample questions or submissions, the units within which answers share a reference and a checklist. The detection floor confirmed that the verdict rules find most of the planted effects it tested (not differences of 0.10 in human agreement on programs; §4.6) and, when both formats share a scale, rarely find effects that are not there (§4.6 gives the exception for different scales), but it was written and scored by the same session that ran the study. In the assessments of software programs, a difference in human agreement smaller than about 0.15 could go undetected. Several estimates were reported per corpus and dimension without correction for multiplicity. The short-answer difference in human agreement and the false-sentence contrast have intervals well away from zero. The key-terms contrast (lower bound +0.014) and the test–retest difference (upper bound −0.001) do not, and could fail a correction for multiplicity.

# 7.5 Conflict of interest

The Learning Design Alliance, my own organization, builds learning tools that grade student work with LLMs, and its choice of rubric format could be informed by this study. The design, the instruments and the analysis were all produced within it. No research team independent of this work has reproduced it. Before publication, an AI agent with no part in the work reproduced every result from the release files alone. The corpora and the human grades were produced by other people. The work was carried out with Claude Code, an Anthropic product; neither model under test is an Anthropic model, and the checklist author and the manipulation checker were OpenAI and Google models.

# 8. Conclusion

For two LLM graders of short-answer assessments and assessments of software programs, replacing a Likert rubric with a checklist of precise yes/no checks was not shown to make scores more reliable: in the short-answer assessments both formats were already near the ceiling of repeatability, and in the assessments of software programs the checklist was less reliable wherever the difference was large enough to be clear. In the short-answer assessments every kind of validity evidence went against it. Its scores agreed less with the human raters, and it under-credited partly and fully correct answers. Written from a reference answer, it mostly checked whether the expected content was present: it barely registered a false claim unless it had checks written to look for errors, and it rewarded key terms used without understanding.

The reliability gains reported for checklists elsewhere were measured on different raters and different content, and a gain in agreement between raters is not a gain in validity. An educator choosing a rubric format for LLM grading should test it against independent human grades and with planted errors before trusting it.

# 9. Data, code and provenance

Data. The study reads two public corpora: the Mohler short-answer corpus (Hugging Face mirror nkazi/MohlerASAG, https://huggingface.co/datasets/nkazi/MohlerASAG) and Menagerie (OSF, https://osf.io/q8jbt), both released under CC BY 4.0. The release file records each file's location and SHA-256. The release publishes no student answer or program text, no short-answer checklist or planted sentence, and no prompt text; the programming checklists, written from the corpus's public rubric, are in the code package (code/studies/measurement/grader-boolean-rubrics/out/checklists.json).

Per-case outputs. per-case-model-outputs.jsonl, beside the release file, holds every grading: ids, human scores, draw membership, each checklist's length and per-check type flags, the perturbation flags, and each call's scores and per-check YES/NO. Every analysis in this paper runs from that file alone.

Code. The release's code/ package holds the two analysis scripts, their outputs, the figure script and the shared helpers they import. code/studies/measurement/grader-boolean-rubrics/boolean.py is the registered study; its docstring is the full record of the design, the floor and its revision. code/studies/measurement/grader-checklist-defects/defects.py is the follow-up. The model calls cannot be re-sent from the release, because the checklists and planted sentences paraphrase the corpus text, which the release does not publish. Every number can be recomputed from the per-case file.

Reproducing the results. reproduce.py, beside the release file, reruns each analysis from the per-case file and compares each output with the published one, byte for byte.

# AI use

I, David Porcaro, orchestrated the development of this report. I asked the questions that drove this benchmark study, pointed the coding agent to methods, articles, and datasets and responded to questions. I supervised errors and made decisions on fixes.

I did not write the methods or code, I did not write the report itself, nor did I review all the prior research cited. I do not claim to have done anything I did not.

I did review every line of the final report to make sure I understood the background, methods and results, and only signed off when I had successfully answered questions about the headline results and findings from the agent.

# Appendix A. Definitions and the detection floor

# A.1 Notation and formulas

This appendix gives the formulas behind the measures in §4.6, for readers who want the exact definitions. The notation is as follows:

  • si,kf,m is the score that model m gave item i in format f on call k (k=1,2).
  • f is either lik (the Likert format) or chk (the checklist).
  • s¯if,m is the mean of the two calls.
  • hi is the mean human score.
  • r(x,y) is Pearson's correlation between two lists of scores over the same items.

Pearson's r is unchanged when either list of scores is multiplied by a positive number or shifted by a constant, so the formats' different score ranges do not affect it. A coarser scale is a different matter: it rounds scores into fewer values, and that can lower r (A.2).

Reliability and human agreement. For each model and format:

Hf,m=r(s¯f,m,h),Rf,m=r(s1f,m,s2f,m),Xf=r(s¯f,Gemini,s¯f,GPT).

Differences between formats. dH and dR are averaged over the two models; dX already uses both. The same differences for a single model, without the average, give the per-model verdicts:

dH=12∑m(Hchk,m−Hlik,m),dR=12∑m(Rchk,m−Rlik,m),dX=Xchk−Xlik.

Planted defects. For each model, D is the mean over the n answers in a set, and the two models are then averaged:

Df=12∑m1n∑i[s¯if,m(planted)−s¯if,m(neutral)],C=Dchk−Dlik.

Which checks registered the defect. For check j of answer i, let yij be the share of the two calls that answered YES, and dij=yij(planted)−yij(neutral) its change. For an answer whose checklist has ni checks, the change in its score is the sum of the change on its error checks (E) and on its presence checks (P):

Dichk=1ni∑jdij=Ei+Pi,Ei=1ni∑j∈errordij,Pi=1ni∑j∉errordij.

E and P are the means of Ei and Pi over answers, averaged over the two models, so D=E+P exactly. On the answers whose checklist has at least one error check, two further measures say how much the error checks mattered. S=E¯/D¯ is the error checks' share of the checklist's loss. K=D¯pres−D¯ re-scores the same answers on their presence checks alone, where Dipres is the mean of dij over the presence checks only. A positive K means that dropping the error checks would have hidden part of the error. E, P, S and K answer the follow-up's questions in §5.3 (Table 5).

By band of human score. The human mean is on 0–5 in the short-answer assessments, so it is divided by 5:

εif=12∑ms¯if,m−hi5,Gb=1|b|∑i∈b(εichk−εilik).

The human score cancels in G, so G is also the mean difference between the two formats' scores in that band.

Intervals and verdicts. Estimates pooled over models are the mean of the two models' estimates on the same bootstrap resample. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 4,000 bootstrap resamples. A difference is clear when 0∉CI95, and otherwise EQUIVALENT when CI90⊂(−δ,δ), with δ = 0.05 for human agreement and 0.03 for reliability. The follow-up's verdicts on P and K follow the same pattern with a margin of ±0.02; E has a one-sided test only (its 95% interval below zero), and the verdict on S asks whether its 95% interval lies above or below one half.

# A.2 The detection floor

The detection floor planted known effects in synthetic graders built on the real draws, human scores and question clusters, and it passed before any model call. Each world in the floor sets the simulated graders' true properties, such as equal reliability or a difference in human agreement of 0.08, and is simulated 200 times; each simulation is a replicate. A gated check is a pass mark set in advance: for example, a world with no difference may produce a clear verdict in at most 10% of replicates, and a world with a planted difference must produce the right verdict in at least 80%. The floor's first version failed three of its gated checks.

One failure was informative about the formats. A format's output grid is the set of scores it can give. The Likert format on a short answer can give 11 (0 to 5 in steps of 0.5), and a checklist of six checks can give 7 (from none to all six answered YES). Two simulated graders with equal true reliability but these two grids produced a spurious "Likert more reliable" test–retest verdict in 20.5% of replicates.

The cause is rounding. A grader's judgment of an answer can fall near the boundary between two possible scores, landing on one side in one grading and on the other side in the next. The fewer the possible scores, the wider the steps between them, and the larger each such jump. So a format with fewer possible scores gives two gradings that agree less, even when the judgment behind them is just as consistent. This is a known property of correlations computed from coarse categories, and it matters most when the correlation would otherwise be high, because little other noise is left for the rounding to hide in (Bollen & Barb, 1981; Aguinis, Pierce & Culpepper, 2009). The registered null world was corrected to give both graders one grid, and the effect of the grid alone was measured in a separate world. With a six-check checklist (seven possible scores) in both corpora, the grid alone gives that spurious verdict in 22.5% (short-answer assessments) and 23.5% (assessments of software programs) of replicates. The program checklists actually used had 10 to 12 checks (11 to 13 possible scores against the Likert format's 14), so the program figure overstates what the grid can explain there.

The other two failures were of power in the assessments of software programs: a difference in human agreement of +0.10 and of −0.10 was detected in 54.5% and 56% of replicates, against a bar of 80%. The revision added ±0.15 worlds, which pass. In the revised floor a difference of ±0.10 is detected in 56–58% of replicates, against 83.5–87.5% for ±0.15. An UNRESOLVED verdict on human agreement in the assessments of software programs therefore does not rule out differences up to about 0.15. In the short-answer assessments ±0.08 is detected in 95–97% of replicates.
